title: NIST AI RMF and the GenAI profile
summary: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary guidance with four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. NIST AI 600-1 adds a Generative AI Profile with twelve risks. It gives a shared vocabulary, not a certificate.
useIf: A customer, board or team needs a common way to describe AI risk work, especially for generative AI.
avoidIf: You need a legal compliance statement or a certifiable standard: this is neither.

explain.md: **AI RMF 1.0** was released on 2023-01-26 and is voluntary. Its four functions are **Govern** (accountability, policy and culture, cross-cutting), **Map** (context, intended use and who is affected), **Measure** (analysing and tracking risk with evidence) and **Manage** (prioritising and acting on risk). NIST states that AI RMF 1.0 is being revised, and on 2026-04-07 it published a concept note for a critical-infrastructure profile, so cite the version you used [[r10]]. The companion **Playbook** offers suggested actions per sub-category. It is neither a checklist nor a set of steps, and NIST says it will be updated after the framework is revised [[tr9]].

**NIST AI 600-1**, the Generative AI Profile, was released on 2024-07-26. It names twelve risks: CBRN information or capabilities, confabulation, dangerous, violent or hateful content, data privacy, environmental impacts, harmful bias and homogenization, human-AI configuration, information integrity, information security, intellectual property, obscene, degrading or abusive content, and value chain and component integration. Prompt injection, including indirect injection, and data poisoning sit under information security [[r11]]. Use it as a **risk checklist for threat models and evals**, not as a rulebook.

explain.title: How the four functions relate
explain.alt: Govern surrounds the loop. Map feeds Measure, Measure feeds Manage, and Manage feeds back into Map.

  ME --> MN[Manage]

pitfalls.symptom: A deck says 'we are NIST certified'
pitfalls.cause: A voluntary framework was treated as a certificate
pitfalls.fix: Say 'aligned with' and show records for each mapped control

pitfalls.symptom: The mapping looks complete but no evidence exists
pitfalls.cause: Controls were listed against subcategories without artefacts
pitfalls.fix: Tie each control to a record: an eval report, an approval log or a review minute

pitfalls.symptom: The 600-1 list is applied evenly to every system
pitfalls.fix: In Map, select the risks that apply per system and justify exclusions

scenarios.title: A customer asks if you are NIST aligned
scenarios.situation: A US enterprise customer's security questionnaire asks whether your AI product is 'NIST AI RMF compliant'.
constraints: You have an eval programme and an incident process
unknowns: Do they want evidence or a statement?
scenarios.question: How do you answer?

options.name: Say you align your practices to the Govern, Map, Measure and Manage functions and AI 600-1 risks, and attach evidence such as eval reports and incident procedures
options.why: It is accurate and verifiable, and speaks the customer's vocabulary.
options.tradeoff: Needs a maintained mapping and evidence pack.

options.name: Reply 'NIST compliant' to close the deal
options.why: There is no compliance regime to claim, and an unsupported claim is a risk.

options.name: Refuse to answer because it is voluntary
options.tradeoff: Loses trust when a short mapping would help.

flips.then: Update the mapping and cite the version.

scenarios.title: A five-person team starting governance
scenarios.situation: A small team ships a GenAI feature to enterprise users in several regions. They have no AI governance programme and a tight budget.
scenarios.question: What do you adopt first?

options.name: Use NIST AI RMF and 600-1 as the working vocabulary and risk checklist, and map EU duties separately where EU users exist
options.why: It is free, voluntary and scalable, and 600-1 gives a concrete GenAI list.
options.tradeoff: It does not satisfy legal or certification demands by itself.

options.name: Start an ISO/IEC 42001 certification programme
options.why: A certificate can unlock enterprise deals.
options.tradeoff: Audit cost and effort are heavy for a tiny team before there is a driver.

options.name: Defer all of it until a customer demands it
options.why: Risks and records are cheaper to build in than to reconstruct.
options.tradeoff: Defer only for prototypes with no real users.

flips.if: The product becomes high-risk under the EU Act

scenarios.takeaway: Vocabulary first, certification when a driver appears.

quiz.q: How many risks does NIST AI 600-1, the Generative AI Profile, list?
quiz.explain: AI 600-1 lists twelve GenAI risks, from CBRN information to value chain and component integration. Prompt injection and data poisoning sit under information security [[r11]].

quiz.q: A customer wants proof of AI governance maturity as a certificate. Which choice fits?
options: NIST AI RMF, because it certifies organizations
quiz.explain: ISO/IEC 42001 is certifiable. NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance with no certification, and the Code of Practice is a voluntary GPAI compliance tool [[r12]].

flashcards.front: What are the four AI RMF functions?
flashcards.back: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Govern is cross-cutting. AI RMF 1.0 was released 2023-01-26 and is voluntary and under revision.
The Generative AI Profile, released 2024-07-26, listing twelve GenAI risks, with prompt injection and data poisoning under information security.
No. It is voluntary guidance. Say aligned and show evidence for each mapped control.
